questiontext.text: In an adjacency matrix M of a graph, what does entry M[i][j] typically hold?

answer.text: 1 (or the weight) if an edge connects i and j, else 0

feedback.text: Correct — the entry records whether (and how strongly) i and j are adjacent.

answer.text: A pointer to the next neighbour of vertex i

feedback.text: That describes an adjacency list node, not a matrix cell.
A single cell records one pair's adjacency, not a vertex's degree.

answer.text: The total number of edges E

feedback.text: E is a global count, not the value of one cell.

generalfeedback.text: M[i][j] is 1 or the edge weight when i and j are adjacent, and 0 otherwise.

questiontext.text: What is the space complexity of an adjacency matrix for a graph with V vertices?

feedback.text: Correct — a V×V table has V^2 cells regardless of the edge count.
That is the adjacency list; the matrix always uses V^2 cells.
The matrix reserves space for all vertex pairs, not just existing edges.
A V×V table is quadratic, not linear, in V.

generalfeedback.text: An adjacency matrix is a V×V table, so it always uses O(V^2) space no matter how many edges exist.

questiontext.text: Using an adjacency matrix, how long does it take to test whether edge (u, v) exists?

feedback.text: Correct — you read the single cell M[u][v] directly.
That is the adjacency list; the matrix indexes directly.
Reading one cell is constant time, not linear.
That is the whole table's size, not the cost of a single lookup.

generalfeedback.text: Direct indexing gives O(1) edge tests — the adjacency matrix's headline advantage.

questiontext.text: Using an adjacency matrix, iterating over all neighbours of a vertex u costs:

answer.text: O(V), because you must scan the entire row of u

feedback.text: Correct — you check every one of the V cells in u's row.
That is the adjacency list; the matrix must scan all V columns.
You cannot list all neighbours in constant time from a matrix.
Scanning one row is O(V), not the whole matrix.

generalfeedback.text: To enumerate u's neighbours you scan all V entries of u's row, costing O(V) even if u has few neighbours.

questiontext.text: An adjacency matrix is a good choice for dense graphs or when fast O(1) edge tests are needed.

feedback.text: Correct — dense graphs use the cells well, and edge lookup is O(1).
Dense graphs and fast edge tests are exactly where the matrix excels.

questiontext.text: An adjacency matrix wastes memory on a sparse graph because it reserves V^2 cells even when E is tiny.

feedback.text: Correct — most cells stay 0 when the graph is sparse.
With few edges most of the V^2 cells are wasted zeros.

questiontext.text: The space used by an adjacency matrix grows on the order of V raised to what power? Answer with a single number.

feedback.text: Correct — O(V^2).
Correct — O(V^2).

questiontext.text: Which statements about the adjacency-matrix representation are true? (select all that apply)

feedback.text: Yes — direct indexing into M[u][v].

answer.text: It uses O(V^2) space regardless of the number of edges

feedback.text: Yes — a full V×V table.

answer.text: Iterating a vertex's neighbours costs only O(degree)

feedback.text: No — you must scan the whole row, costing O(V).

answer.text: It is the most space-efficient choice for very sparse graphs

feedback.text: No — it wastes space on sparse graphs; adjacency lists are better there.

generalfeedback.text: Adjacency matrix: O(1) edge tests, O(V^2) space, O(V) neighbour scans, and wasteful on sparse graphs (best for dense ones).
